content: The treatment of pharyngeal gonorrhea with a single oral dose of cefixime was studied by McMillan and Young in 2007, demonstrating its efficacy in addressing this specific infection. Similarly, Megran et al. in 1990 compared single-dose oral cefixime to a combination of amoxicillin and probenecid for treating uncomplicated gonorrhea in men, highlighting the effectiveness of cefixime as a monotherapy. In 1984, Meheus et al. evaluated the use of spectinomycin and procaine penicillin for treating gonorrhea in males in the Central African Republic, providing insights into the regional management of the disease. Meyer-Rohn, in 1974, explored the use of spectinomycin for gonorrhea treatment, emphasizing its rapid therapeutic action. Mogabgab and Lutz conducted a randomized study in 1994 comparing cefotaxime and ceftriaxone for uncomplicated gonorrhea, underscoring the clinical utility of both antibiotics. Monayar et al. in 1987 investigated the epidemiology and treatment of non-PPNG (penicillinase-producing Neisseria gonorrhoeae) strains in Córdoba, Argentina, analyzing auxotypes, susceptibility profiles, and plasmid characteristics of urethral isolates. Morrison et al. in 1997 compared grepafloxacin and cefixime as single-dose therapies for uncomplicated gonorrhea in women, demonstrating the potential of both agents. Mroczkowski et al. in 1993 evaluated the efficacy of a single 250 mg intramuscular injection of trospectomycin sulfate versus ceftriaxone sodium for gonococcal infections, providing comparative data on these treatments. Murata et al. in 2008 assessed the use of a single 1 g dose of ceftriaxone for urogenital and pharyngeal infections caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, confirming its effectiveness. Niunikova et al. in 1975 studied the treatment of gonorrheal urethritis in men using kanamycin and vibramycin, offering alternative therapeutic options. Odugbemi et al. in 1993 evaluated a single oral dose of azithromycin for treating susceptible sexually transmitted diseases, highlighting its utility in a multicenter open evaluation. Pabst et al. in 1989 conducted a multicenter comparative study of enoxacin and ceftriaxone for uncomplicated gonorrhea, providing evidence for their relative efficacy. Pandhi et al. in 1989 examined the efficacy of gentamicin in treating gonococcal urethritis, while Panikabutra et al. in 1983 explored cefaclor and cefamandole as alternatives to spectinomycin for uncomplicated gonorrhea in men. In 1985, Panikabutra et al. conducted a randomized comparative study of ceftriaxone and spectinomycin for gonorrhea, further expanding treatment options. Porter and Rutherford in 1977 evaluated spectinomycin hydrochloride (Trobicin) for uncomplicated gonorrhea, confirming its clinical utility. Rajan et al. in 1982 studied ceftriaxone for treating both ordinary and penicillinase-producing strains of Neisseria gonorrhoeae, demonstrating its broad-spectrum efficacy. Ratnam et al. in 1982 compared penicillin and spectinomycin for gonococcal urethritis, while Reggiani and Cremonesi in 1983 reported on five years of experience with spectinomycin for gonorrhea treatment. Rompalo et al. in 1994 compared intramuscular and oral treatments for uncomplicated gonorrhea, providing data on patient outcomes. Rustonjee et al. in 2002 conducted a randomized controlled trial comparing azithromycin to doxycycline/ciprofloxacin for syndromic management of sexually transmitted infections in resource-poor settings, emphasizing the practicality of azithromycin. Sands in 1980 focused on the treatment of anorectal gonorrhea infections in men, providing targeted therapeutic insights. Schumacher and Ghanem in 2013 compared retreatment rates for uncomplicated gonorrhea using ceftriaxone with azithromycin versus ceftriaxone with doxycycline, highlighting differences in treatment outcomes. Shams-ur-Rehman et al. in 2009 evaluated the clinical efficacy of various drugs for gonorrhea treatment, offering a comprehensive analysis of therapeutic options. Shi in 2000 compared sparfloxacin and spectinomycin for gonorrhea treatment, while Steingrimsson et al. in 1990 studied azithromycin for sexually transmitted diseases, including gonorrhea. In 1994, Steingrimsson et al. further evaluated single-dose azithromycin for gonorrhea and infections caused by C. trachomatis and U. urealyticum in men. Stratigos et al. in 1973 assessed spectinomycin hydrochloride for gonorrhea treatment, while Swanson et al. in 2001 evaluated single-dose azithromycin therapy for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis in STD clinic attendees. Takahashi et al. in 2014 studied the clinical efficacy of a single two-gram dose of azithromycin extended-release for male urethritis. Tian and Dong in 2002 reported on ceftriaxone for treating gonorrhea in 115 patients, while Tupasi et al. in 1983 compared cefuroxime, thiamphenicol, spectinomycin, and penicillin G for uncomplicated infections caused by penicillinase-producing Neisseria gonorrhoeae. In 1984, Tupasi et al. conducted a comparative trial of thiamphenicol, penicillin, and spectinomycin for gonococcal infections. Turanova et al. in 1975 studied the effectiveness of kanamycin for gonorrhea in women, while Tuzas and Hatos in 1973 evaluated spectinomycin hydrochloride (Trobicin) for male urethral gonorrhea. Verdon et al. in 1993 assessed single doses of 200 mg cefixime for uncomplicated gonorrhea, confirming its efficacy. Waugh in 1993 conducted an open study on the safety and efficacy of a single oral dose of azithromycin for uncomplicated gonorrhea in men and women. Willcox in 1974 evaluated spectinomycin for gonorrhea in males, while Wójtowicz et al. in 1990 studied the incidence and treatment outcomes of beta-lactamase-positive gonorrhea with spectinomycin. Yoon et al. in 1988 compared kanamycin and gentamicin for uncomplicated male gonococcal urethritis, while Zajdowicz et al. in 1983 compared ceftriaxone and cefoxitin for penicillin-resistant gonococcal urethritis. Zhou et al. in 2000 studied etimicin sulfate and spectinomycin for gonorrhea treatment, providing additional therapeutic options.
